entity_or_polity: Alkaline hydrothermal vent FeS/silicate mineral pore cluster
source: Martin & Russell (2003) Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 358:59; Kelley et al. (2005) Science 307:1428; Lane & Martin (2012) Cell 151:1406
note: Model scenario for prebiotic Hadean vent chimneys (Lost City carbonate towers host porous networks with ~10^3-10^6 micrometer-scale chambers per cm^3); no fossil group count exists.

entity_or_polity: Early Eoarchean prokaryotic biofilm microcolony
source: Flemming & Wuertz (2019) Nat. Rev. Microbiol. 17:247; Moody et al. (2024) Nat. Ecol. Evol. 8:1654; Allwood et al. (2006) Nature 441:714
note: Living surface-attached prokaryotic microcolonies contain 10^5-10^8 cells prior to macroscopic stromatolite lamination; unit here is single microbial cells.

entity_or_polity: Paleoarchean anaerobic syntrophic microbial mat
source: Allwood et al. (2006) Nature 441:714; Flemming & Wuertz (2019) Nat. Rev. Microbiol. 17:247; Waters & Bassler (2005) Annu. Rev. Cell Dev. Biol. 21:319
note: Strelley Pool (~3.43 Ga) and Buck Reef (~3.42 Ga) microbial mats; living anaerobic syntrophic biofilms pack 10^8-10^10 cells/cm^3 coupled over millimeter-to-centimeter diffusion scales.

entity_or_polity: Cyanobacterial stromatolite biofilm mat
published_estimate_range: 10^8 - 10^11 cells per coherent mat signaling domain
source: Bosak et al. (2013) Annu. Rev. Earth Planet. Sci. 41:21; Prindle et al. (2015) Nature 527:59; Flemming & Wuertz (2019) Nat. Rev. Microbiol. 17:247
note: Dense phototrophic stromatolite mats reach ~10^9-10^10 cells/cm^3; K+ ion-channel and quorum-sensing waves coordinate ~10^8-10^10 cells across millimeter-to-decimeter patches. Unit is prokaryotic cells (exceeding modern 8.1x10^9 human headcount because cells, not metazoans, are counted).

entity_or_polity: Cryoconite and sub-ice aerotolerant microbial mat
source: Anesio et al. (2009) Glob. Change Biol. 15:955; Langford et al. (2010) Ann. Glaciol. 51:87; Hoffman et al. (2017) Sci. Adv. 3:e1600983
note: Living glacial cryoconite granules and sub-ice cyanobacterial mats hold ~10^8-10^9 cells/g wet sediment, providing an analog for Huronian Snowball refugia.

entity_or_polity: Paleoproterozoic aerobic macro-biofilm / Francevillian colonial sheet
published_estimate_range: 10^8 - 10^11 prokaryotic cells per centimeter-scale colonial sheet
source: El Albani et al. (2010) Nature 466:100; Flemming & Wuertz (2019) Nat. Rev. Microbiol. 17:247
note: 2.1 Ga Francevillian pyritized lobate sheets (1-12 cm across) interpreted as coordinated colonial macro-biofilms or early multicellular aggregates (~10^9-10^10 microbial-scale cells).

entity_or_polity: Syntrophic archaeal-bacterial endosymbiotic consortium & early eukaryotic bloom
source: Imachi et al. (2020) Nature 577:519; Boetius et al. (2000) Nature 407:623; Knoll (2014) Cold Spring Harb. Perspect. Biol. 6:a016121
note: Drop from 10^10 (at 2.1 Ga) to 10^8 marks an ontological shift from prokaryotic stromatolites (which persisted) to larger-celled (~10-100x volume) syntrophic/eukaryotic consortia.

entity_or_polity: Mesoproterozoic benthic plastid-algal mat & acritarch bloom
published_estimate_range: 10^6 - 10^9 eukaryotic algal cells per bloom/mat patch
source: Javaux, Knoll & Walter (2001) Nature 412:66; Bengtson et al. (2017) PLoS Biol. 15:e2000735
note: 1.5-1.6 Ga Roper/Gaoyuzhuang/Rafatazmia eukaryotic algae and acritarchs; 10^8 reflects nucleated cells in a benthic mat or local bloom (stromatolite bacterial mats still held >=10^10 cells).

entity_or_polity: Multicellular clonal red algal thallus (Bangiomorpha) / social amoeba grex
published_estimate_range: 10^3 - 2x10^5 cells per clonal filament or fruiting aggregate
source: Butterfield (2000) Paleobiology 26:386; Bonner (2009) The Social Amoebae, Princeton Univ. Press
note: Ontological shift at 1.1 Ga: census switches from free-living microbial mat cells (10^8-10^10) to cells inside a single clonal multicellular thallus/grex (Bangiomorpha filaments ~10^3-10^4 cells; Dictyostelium slugs 10^4-2x10^5 cells).

entity_or_polity: Early Tonian mycelial fungal network & colonial choanoflagellate/algal tuft
source: Loron et al. (2019) Nature 570:232; Fairclough, Dayel & King (2010) Curr. Biol. 20:R875; Butterfield (2009) Paleobiology 35:1
note: ~1.0-0.9 Ga Ourasphaira fungal-like microfossils and colonial opisthokont/algal thalli; 10^6 counts compartments in a centimeter-scale mycelial network.

entity_or_polity: Cryogenian Snowball meltwater algal & stem-sponge cell aggregate
source: Love et al. (2009) Nature 457:718; Hoffman et al. (2017) Sci. Adv. 3:e1600983; Simpson, Perina & Leys (2024) J. Exp. Biol.
note: Small multicellular sponge-grade and cryophilic algal aggregates (~10^4-10^6 cells) surviving in Sturtian sea-ice brine channels and cryoconite pools.

entity_or_polity: Post-Marinoan demosponge aquiferous sheet
source: Leys & Meech (2006) Can. J. Zool. 84:288; Elliott & Leys (2007) J. Exp. Biol. 210:3736; Yin et al. (2015) PNAS 112:E1453
note: Living cm-to-dm demosponges coordinate whole-body oscular contractions via glutamate/Ca2+ waves across ~10^7-10^8 pinacocyte and choanocyte cells; unit is somatic cells in one sponge.

entity_or_polity: Ediacaran Avalon rangeomorph frond (Charnia) & epithelial sheet
published_estimate_range: 10^6 - 10^8 somatic cells per meter-scale frond (or 10^2-10^4 fronds per bedding community)
source: Narbonne (2004) Science 305:1141; Mitchell et al. (2015) Nature 524:343; Sperling & Vinther (2010) Evol. Dev. 12:201
note: 1e7 represents somatic cells coordinated within a decimeter-to-meter Charnia/Fractofusus frond; ecological bedding-plane clusters at Mistaken Point number 10^2-10^4 fronds.

entity_or_polity: Ediacaran colonial cnidarian polyp colony & grazing bilaterian aggregation
source: Liu et al. (2014) Proc. R. Soc. B 281:20141202; Evans et al. (2020) PNAS 117:7845; Mackie, Pugh & Purcell (1987) Adv. Mar. Biol. 24:97
note: Ontological shift at 555 Ma: census switches from somatic cells per body (10^7 at 575 Ma) to individual zooids/metazoans in a colony or grazing swarm (~10^3-10^4).

entity_or_polity: Fortunian archaeocyathid/calcimicrobial reef & bioturbating worm aggregation
source: Rowland & Shapiro (2002) Palaios 17:171; Mangano & Buatois (2014) Earth-Sci. Rev. 130:106; Wood (1999) Reef Evolution, Oxford Univ. Press
note: Early Cambrian modular reef consortia and dense Treptichnus/worm burrow beds (~10^3-10^4 individuals/m^2 across local shoals).

entity_or_polity: Cambrian trilobite migratory queue / pelagic arthropod swarm & siphonophore colony
source: Vannier et al. (2019) Sci. Rep. 9:14981; Paterson et al. (2011) Nature 474:634; Mackie, Pugh & Purcell (1987) Adv. Mar. Biol. 24:97
note: Fossil trilobite single-file queues preserve 10-10^2 individuals per slab, while pelagic bivalved arthropod/krill-analog swarms and benthic trilobite mass-molt beds scale to ~10^4-10^5.

entity_or_polity: Ordovician bryozoan/tabulate coral reef colony & pelagic graptolite rhabdosome
published_estimate_range: 10^3 - 10^4 zooids per graptolite rhabdosome; 10^4 - 10^7 zooids/polyps per bryozoan/coral colony
source: Lidgard et al. (2012) PNAS 109:10756; Hughes (1989) A Functional Biology of Clonal Animals; Rigby (1993) Paleobiology 19:215
note: 1e5 matches large modular bryozoan and tabulate/rugose coral colonies in Middle Ordovician reefs (individual colonies span 10^4-10^7 cloned zooids).

entity_or_polity: Late Ordovician schooling ostracoderm agnathans & eurypterid mass-mating aggregation
published_estimate_range: 10^3 - 10^6 schooling jawless fish / mass-molting arthropods; up to 10^6 reef zooids
source: Vrazo & Braddy (2011) Palaeogeogr. Palaeoclimatol. Palaeoecol. 311:63; Sansom et al. (2015) Palaeontology 58:267; Lidgard et al. (2012) PNAS 109:10756
note: Mass mortality slabs of ostracoderms and eurypterid molt/spawning congregations plus persistent colonial bryozoan/coral reefs (~10^5-10^6).

entity_or_polity: Hirnantian refugial deep-shelf brachiopod bed & surviving bryozoan colony
source: Harper, Hammarlund & Rasmussen (2014) Palaeogeogr. Palaeoclimatol. Palaeoecol. 389:43; Sheehan (2001) Annu. Rev. Earth Planet. Sci. 29:331
note: End-Ordovician glaciation wiped out warm-shelf coral-stromatoporoid reefs, contracting largest modular/benthic collectives to ~10^4.

entity_or_polity: Early Silurian re-radiating tabulate-stromatoporoid reef & acanthodian shoal
source: Copper & Jin (2012) Earth-Sci. Rev. 114:129;Lidgard et al. (2012) PNAS 109:10756
note: Llandovery recovery of colonial tabulate corals, bryozoans, and early jawed acanthodian shoals (~10^5).

entity_or_polity: Silurian myelinated gnathostome fish school & giant Silurian coral-stromatoporoid reef
published_estimate_range: 10^4 - 10^7 schooling fish or clonal reef polyps
source: Pitcher & Parrish (1993) Behaviour of Teleost Fishes; Marras et al. (2015) Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 69:219; Copper (2002) Phanerozoic Reef Patterns
note: Lateral-line hydrodynamic schooling in jawed fishes and Wenlock-Ludlow barrier reefs reach ~10^6 coupled individuals/polyps.

entity_or_polity: Early Devonian arbuscular mycorrhizal-vascular plant clonal network
published_estimate_range: 10^2 - 10^5 clonal ramets/root-linked stems (census 10^8 counts root tips/hyphal nodes rather than whole plants)
source: Remy et al. (1994) PNAS 91:11841; Karst, Jones & Hoeksema (2023) Nat. Ecol. Evol. 7:501; Grant, Mitton & Linhart (1992) Nature 360:216
note: Discrepancy note: Rhynie chert (407 Ma) proves glomeromycorrhizal root symbiosis, but the communication-networks ledger gives 10-10^4 root-linked stems (even the modern Pando aspen clone is ~47,000 stems), and Karst et al. (2023) critique 'wood-wide web' signaling claims. Census 10^8 is only plausible if counting hyphal/root-tip junctions or marine fish shoals.

entity_or_polity: Late Devonian surviving pelagic fish shoal
source: Sallan & Coates (2010) PNAS 107:10131; Copper (2002) SEPM Spec. Publ. 72:181; Pitcher & Parrish (1993) Behaviour of Teleost Fishes
note: Kellwasser crisis collapsed >90% of Frasnian stromatoporoid-tabulate reef ecosystems, leaving pelagic actinopterygian/chondrichthyan shoals (~10^6) as largest collectives.

entity_or_polity: Famennian actinopterygian fish shoals & Archaeopteris floodplain forest stands
source: Sallan & Coates (2010) PNAS 107:10131; Stein et al. (2020) Curr. Biol. 30:485; Makris et al. (2009) Science 323:1734
note: Post-extinction radiation of ray-finned (actinopterygian) fishes makes pelagic marine shoals (~10^6-10^7) the largest mobile collectives alongside early Archaeopteris forests.

entity_or_polity: Carboniferous coal-swamp lycopsid stand & proto-social blattopteran/insect aggregation
published_estimate_range: 10^4 - 10^6 gregarious insects or clonal swamp-forest stems (marine fish shoals still 10^6 - 10^7)
source: DiMichele, Phillips & Peppers (2001) Annu. Rev. Earth Planet. Sci. 29:461; Legendre et al. (2015) Curr. Biol. 25:1928
note: Focuses on terrestrial coal-swamp guilds (~10^6); note pelagic marine fish shoals from 365 Ma did not shrink in the Carboniferous.

entity_or_polity: Late Permian herding dicynodont synapsids & Glossopteris woodland stands
published_estimate_range: 10^2 - 10^5 herding terrestrial vertebrates (marine fish/invertebrate shoals still >=10^6)
source: Fiorelli et al. (2013) Sci. Rep. 3:3348; Smith & Ward (2001) Geology 29:1147; Viglietti et al. (2021) PNAS 118:e2017045118
note: Census 10^5 tracks terrestrial amniote herds/communal nesting grounds on dry Pangaea rather than marine pelagic fish shoals.

entity_or_polity: End-Permian Lystrosaurus burrow aggregations & disaster fungal mats
source: Botha-Brink (2017) Sci. Rep. 7:17912; Viglietti et al. (2021) PNAS 118:e2017045118; Chen & Benton (2012) Nat. Geosci. 5:375
note: 90% marine/terrestrial extinction wiped out Paleozoic reefs and collapsed pelagic shoals; 10^4 reflects disaster-fauna Lystrosaurus aggregations.

entity_or_polity: Early-Middle Triassic communal-burrowing cynodonts & recovering ammonoid/fish shoals
published_estimate_range: 10 - 10^3 cynodont burrow clusters; 10^4 - 10^6 pelagic ammonoid/actinopterygian shoals
source: Fernandez et al. (2013) PLoS ONE 8:e64978; Brayard et al. (2009) Science 325:1118
note: Individual Thrinaxodon burrows hold small kin groups, while recovering Olenekian-Anisian ammonoid and ray-finned fish shoals scale to 10^4-10^6.

entity_or_polity: Late Triassic prosauropod (Plateosaurus/Mussaurus) nesting & herding colonies
published_estimate_range: 10^2 - 10^4 dinosaurs per herd/rookery; 10^5 - 10^6 marine fish/ammonoid shoals
source: Pol et al. (2021) Sci. Rep. 11:21132; Sander (1992) Palaeontol. Z. 66:259
note: Mussaurus/Plateosaurus bonebeds document age-segregated colonial nesting and herds of 10^2-10^4 on land; 10^5 reflects maximum regional migratory herds or marine shoals.

entity_or_polity: Norian-Rhaetian coelophysoid bonebed aggregations & prosauropod rookeries
source: Schwartz & Gillette (1994) J. Vertebr. Paleontol. 14:510; Pol et al. (2021) Sci. Rep. 11:21132
note: Ghost Ranch preserves >=1,000 Coelophysis in one monodominant deposit; 10^5 spans largest regional archosaur herds / marine shoals.

entity_or_polity: End-Triassic CAMP crisis refugial archosaur & fish aggregations
source: Blackburn et al. (2013) Science 340:941; Olsen et al. (2002) Science 296:1305
note: CAMP hyperthermal collapsed Triassic reef and terrestrial faunas, transiently shrinking large herd/shoal sizes (~10^4).

entity_or_polity: Early Jurassic pelagic teleost (leptolepid) fish schools & marine reptile pods
source: Arratia (1997) Mesozoic Fishes; Makris et al. (2009) Science 323:1734; Mizumoto, Miyata & Pratt (2019) Proc. R. Soc. B 286:20190891
note: Stem-teleost radiation establishes large pelagic fish schools (10^6 central; living oceanic herring shoals reach 2.5x10^8 in Makris et al. 2009).

entity_or_polity: Late Jurassic migratory sauropod herds & stem-termite wood-dwelling colonies
published_estimate_range: 10^2 - 10^4 sauropods per trackway herd; 10^3 - 10^5 stem-isopteran termites (marine teleost shoals still >=10^6)
source: Myers & Fiorillo (2009) Palaeogeogr. Palaeoclimatol. Palaeoecol. 274:122; Engel, Grimaldi & Krishna (2009) Am. Mus. Novit. 3650
note: Discrepancy note: census drops from 10^6 (185 Ma marine fish) to 10^5 (150 Ma terrestrial herds/early termites) because it shifts focus from pelagic fish to land collectives.

entity_or_polity: Early Cretaceous social termite colonies & iguanodont/ornithopod dinosaur herds
source: Engel, Grimaldi & Krishna (2009) Am. Mus. Novit. 3650; Bourguignon et al. (2015) Mol. Biol. Evol. 32:406
note: Oldest fossil termites (Baissatermes, Meiatermes ~130-135 Ma) mark the rise of eusocial insect colonies (~10^4-5x10^5 workers).

entity_or_polity: Late Cretaceous eusocial ant and termite colonies & hadrosaur mega-rookeries
published_estimate_range: 10^4 - 10^6 workers per eusocial colony; ~10^4 Maiasaura/hadrosaurs in nesting grounds
source: Moreau et al. (2006) Science 312:101; Barden & Grimaldi (2016) Curr. Biol. 26:515; Horner (1982) Nature 297:675; Burchill & Moreau (2016) Insectes Soc. 63:291
note: Crown-group ants and termites diversify alongside angiosperm forests (~10^5-10^6 colony scale; note pelagic teleost shoals >=10^7 also coexisted, while tightly integrated reproductive superorganisms peaked around ~10^6).

entity_or_polity: K-Pg boundary subterranean termite & ant colonies
source: Robertson et al. (2004) Geol. Soc. Am. Bull. 116:760; Burchill & Moreau (2016) Insectes Soc. 63:291; Schultheiss et al. (2022) PNAS 119:e2201550119
note: Subterranean eusocial insect colonies buffered the Chicxulub thermal pulse and impact winter via underground detritus/seed stores (~5x10^5).

entity_or_polity: Early Paleocene eusocial ant/termite colonies & neornithine bird flocks
source: Hölldobler & Wilson (2009) The Superorganisms, W. W. Norton; Burchill & Moreau (2016) Insectes Soc. 63:291
note: Rapid recovery of crown-ant and termite superorganisms in regrowing Paleocene tropical rainforests (~10^6).

entity_or_polity: Eocene fungus-farming termite mounds (Macrotermitinae) & early attine ants
source: Bourguignon et al. (2015) Mol. Biol. Evol. 32:406; Schultz & Brady (2008) PNAS 105:5435; King, Ocko & Mahadevan (2015) PNAS 112:11589; Darlington (1984) Insectes Soc. 31:383
note: Mature living Macrotermes mounds house 1-3 million (up to ~5M) sterile workers/soldiers under a single royal pair. Note: molecular clocks place Termitidae diversification closer to ~50-30 Ma (Macrotermitinae ~30-25 Ma) and fungus-farming attine ants at ~50-60 Ma.

entity_or_polity: Oligocene army/driver ant & Macrotermes superorganism colonies (plus avian flocks)
published_estimate_range: 10^6 - 10^7 eusocial workers per colony; 10^4 - 10^6 birds in murmurations
source: Brady et al. (2014) Curr. Biol. 24:1190; Burchill & Moreau (2016) Insectes Soc. 63:291; Ballerini et al. (2008) PNAS 105:1232
note: Doryline army/driver ants (Old/New World clades diverging ~50-30 Ma; Brady et al. 2014) and Macrotermitinae mounds reach ~3-10M workers per colony.

entity_or_polity: Early Miocene higher-attine/leafcutter ant precursors, Dorylus driver ants & Macrotermes
source: Branstetter et al. (2017) Proc. R. Soc. B 284:20170095; Schultz & Brady (2008) PNAS 105:5435; Hölldobler & Wilson (2010) The Leafcutter Ants, W. W. Norton
note: Leaf-cutting genera Atta and Acromyrmex originate ~15-19 Ma during Miocene savanna expansion (Branstetter et al. 2017), scaling fungus gardens toward multi-million-worker nests.

entity_or_polity: Mature leafcutter ant megacolony (Atta)
published_estimate_range: 5x10^6 - 8x10^6 workers per single-queen Atta colony (up to 2x10^7 in Dorylus driver ants; 2.5x10^8 in oceanic herring shoals)
source: Hölldobler & Wilson (2009) The Superorganisms; Hölldobler & Wilson (2010) The Leafcutter Ants; Burchill & Moreau (2016) Insectes Soc. 63:291
note: Anchored to single-queen Atta cephalotes / Atta sexdens megacolonies (5-8M workers; great ape fission-fusion communities in the same epoch hold ~30-120 individuals).

entity_or_polity: Mature leafcutter ant megacolony (Atta) alongside ~10^6 ungulate herds & ~30-50 hominin bands
source: Hölldobler & Wilson (2010) The Leafcutter Ants; Holdo, Holt & Fryxell (2009) Am. Nat. 173:431; Dunbar (1993) Behav. Brain Sci. 16:681
note: 8e6 continues to track eusocial Atta superorganisms while bipedal hominins live in ~30-50 member bands.

entity_or_polity: Mature leafcutter ant megacolony (Atta) alongside ~40-60 Australopithecus bands
source: Hölldobler & Wilson (2010) The Leafcutter Ants; Dunbar (1993) Behav. Brain Sci. 16:681
note: 8e6 tracks Atta megacolonies; hominin bands remain ~5 orders of magnitude smaller (~50).

entity_or_polity: Mature leafcutter ant megacolony (Atta) alongside ~50-80 early Homo bands
source: Hölldobler & Wilson (2010) The Leafcutter Ants; Dunbar (1993) Behav. Brain Sci. 16:681
note: 8e6 tracks Atta megacolonies while Oldowan Homo habilis bands average ~50-80 individuals.

entity_or_polity: Mature leafcutter ant megacolony (Atta) alongside ~60-100 Homo erectus bands
source: Hölldobler & Wilson (2010) The Leafcutter Ants; Aiello & Dunbar (1993) Curr. Anthropol. 34:184
note: 8e6 tracks Atta megacolonies; neocortex-predicted group size for Homo erectus rises to ~90-110 (Aiello & Dunbar 1993).

entity_or_polity: Mature leafcutter ant megacolony (Atta) alongside ~100-150 archaic Homo kin networks
source: Hölldobler & Wilson (2010) The Leafcutter Ants; Dunbar (1993) Behav. Brain Sci. 16:681; Pearce, Stringer & Dunbar (2013) Proc. R. Soc. B 280:20130168
note: 8e6 tracks Atta megacolonies; Middle Pleistocene hominin cranial capacity reaches Dunbar's ~120-150 personal-network limit.

entity_or_polity: Mature leafcutter ant megacolony (Atta) alongside ~150 early Homo sapiens band/clan networks
published_estimate_range: 5x10^6 - 8x10^6 Atta workers (early H. sapiens residential bands ~35, clans ~150)
source: Hölldobler & Wilson (2010) The Leafcutter Ants; Hill et al. (2011) Science 331:1286; Dunbar (1993) Behav. Brain Sci. 16:681
note: 8e6 tracks Atta megacolonies; living hunter-gatherer residential bands average ~28-35 within ~150-person clans (Hill et al. 2011).

entity_or_polity: Mature leafcutter ant megacolony (Atta) alongside ~500-1,000 symbolic H. sapiens meta-bands
source: Hölldobler & Wilson (2010) The Leafcutter Ants; Hill et al. (2011) Science 331:1286; d'Errico et al. (2005) J. Hum. Evol. 48:3
note: 8e6 tracks Atta megacolonies while shell-bead/ochre exchange links human bands into ~500-1,500 person regional tribes.

entity_or_polity: Mature leafcutter ant megacolony (Atta) alongside ~1,000-2,000 Upper Paleolithic ethnolinguistic tribes
source: Hölldobler & Wilson (2010) The Leafcutter Ants; Bird et al. (2019) Sci. Adv. 5:eaav7939; Hill et al. (2011) Science 331:1286
note: Last moment where census reports Atta (8e6) before switching to human settlements at 8000 BCE (10 ka).

entity_or_polity: Pre-Pottery Neolithic sedentary farming villages (Jericho, 'Ain Ghazal, Çatalhöyük)
published_estimate_range: 500 - 3,000 residents in PPNB villages (up to 3,500-8,000 at peak Çatalhöyük c. 6500 BCE; Atta ants still 5-8M!)
source: Kuijt (2000) J. Anthropol. Archaeol. 19:75; Cessford (2005) Inhabiting Çatalhöyük; Hodder (2006) The Leopard's Tale
note: MAJOR DISCREPANCY FLAGGED: Census drops 4,000-fold from 8.0e6 (45 ka Atta ants) to 2.0e3 (8000 BCE human villages) because the metric silently switches from 'largest biological colony on Earth' to 'largest human settlement/polity'. Atta leafcutter ants (5-8M) and Dorylus driver ants (10-20M) still existed from 8000 BCE through 1300 BCE!

entity_or_polity: Chalcolithic chiefdoms & proto-urban temple towns (Ubaid / Early-Middle Uruk / Susa / Trypillia)
published_estimate_range: 10,000 - 25,000 people per proto-urban settlement/chiefdom (Atta ants still 5-8M)
source: Algaze (2008) Ancient Mesopotamia at the Dawn of Civilization, Univ. Chicago Press; Flannery & Marcus (2012) The Creation of Inequality; Müller, Rassmann & Videiko (2016) Trypillia Mega-Sites
note: Matches Ubaid-to-Middle-Uruk Mesopotamian irrigation polities and Cucuteni-Trypillia mega-settlements (~10,000-20,000 residents); still below Atta's 8M until 500 BCE.

entity_or_polity: Early Dynastic unified Egypt (First Dynasty) & Uruk city-state
published_estimate_range: 40,000 - 50,000 (Uruk city proper); 500,000 - 1,200,000 (First Dynasty unified Nile state c. 3000 BCE)
source: Nissen (1988) The Early History of the Ancient Near East; Algaze (2008) Ancient Mesopotamia at the Dawn of Civilization; Butzer (1976) Early Hydraulic Civilization in Egypt; Taagepera (1978) Soc. Sci. Res. 7:108
note: Uruk city held ~40,000-50,000 people (~80,000-100,000 with hinterland), while newly unified First Dynasty Egypt governed ~0.8-1.2M along the Nile ( justifying 5e5-1e6 for a state, though census text mentions 'Akkad', which actually dates to ~2334 BCE, 700 yr later, and Atta ants still had 5-8M workers).

entity_or_polity: New Kingdom Egypt (18th-19th Dynasty), Late Shang China & Hittite Empire
source: Butzer (1976) Early Hydraulic Civilization in Egypt; Kemp (2006) Ancient Egypt: Anatomy of a Civilization; Keightley (1999) Cambridge History of Ancient China; Taagepera (1978) Soc. Sci. Res. 7:108
note: New Kingdom Egypt under Amenhotep III / Ramesses II governed ~3-4.5M people (including Nubian/Levantine provinces) and Late Shang China ~4-5M; still slightly below 8M Atta colonies.

entity_or_polity: Achaemenid Persian Empire under Darius I
source: Taagepera (1979) Soc. Sci. Hist. 3:115; Wiesehöfer (1996) Ancient Persia; Scheidel (2019) Escape from Rome, Princeton Univ. Press; Turchin et al. (2013) PNAS 110:16384
note: First human polity that unambiguously exceeds every eusocial insect colony (8M Atta, 20M Dorylus): Achaemenid Persia integrated Egypt, Mesopotamia, Anatolia, Iran, and Indus borderlands (~20-35M subjects; note viral 50M internet claims are rejected by modern demographers since HYDE global population at 500 BCE was ~171M).

entity_or_polity: Maurya & Seleucid Empires at 300 BCE; Western Han (2 CE census) & High Roman Empire in Classical window
published_estimate_range: 2.0x10^7 - 5.0x10^7 at 300 BCE (Maurya/Seleucid); 57,671,400 - 59,594,978 (Han 2 CE census) & 5.5x10^7 - 7.0x10^7 (Roman peak c. 160 CE)
source: Ban Gu (c. 82 CE) Book of Han (Hanshu) ch. 28B; Bielenstein (1947) BMFEA 19:125; Scheidel (2007) Cambridge Economic History of the Greco-Roman World; Dyson (2018) A Population History of India; Taagepera (1979) Soc. Sci. Hist. 3:115
note: Chronological note: At exact 300 BCE, neither the Han Dynasty (founded 202 BCE) nor the Roman Empire (27 BCE; Republic had ~4M in 300 BCE) existed yet—the largest 300 BCE polity was Chandragupta's Maurya Empire (~30-50M, Dyson 2018) or Seleucid Empire (~15-25M). Census 6.0e7 reflects the Classical peak inside the 300 BCE-400 CE span: the 2 CE Hanshu census recorded 57,671,400 (or 59,594,978) individuals in 12.23M households, and Rome peaked at ~55-70M (Scheidel 2007).

entity_or_polity: Eastern + Western Roman Empire / Gupta Empire / Sasanian Empire (400 CE)
published_estimate_range: 4.0x10^7 - 5.0x10^7 (combined Theodosian Roman halves c. 395-400 CE; ~20-25M Eastern Roman alone); 3.0x10^7 - 5.0x10^7 (Gupta sphere)
source: Scheidel (2007) Cambridge Economic History of the Greco-Roman World; McEvedy & Jones (1978) Atlas of World Population History; Dyson (2018) A Population History of India; Taagepera (1979) Soc. Sci. Hist. 3:115
note: In 395 CE the Roman Empire split administratively into Eastern (~22-25M) and Western (~20-22M) courts (~45M combined); Chandragupta II's Gupta Empire and tributaries in India held ~30-50M. Note census text says 'Tang precursor', though Tang began in 618 CE (Northern Wei/Eastern Jin held ~25-30M in 400 CE).

entity_or_polity: Northern Song Dynasty China
published_estimate_range: 6.0x10^7 - 1.0x10^8 subjects (rising from ~60-70M in 1000 CE to ~100-120M by 1100 CE)
source: Durand (1960) Popul. Stud. 13:209; McEvedy & Jones (1978) Atlas of World Population History; Maddison (2001) The World Economy: A Millennial Perspective, OECD; Chaffee (2015) Cambridge History of China Vol. 5
note: Song household registers passed 20 million households (~100-110M people) in the late 11th century (c. 1080-1110 CE; in 1000 CE proper, Song China held ~60-80M before peaking above 100M within the 1000-1450 CE span).

entity_or_polity: Ming Dynasty China
published_estimate_range: 8.5x10^7 - 1.3x10^8 subjects (official fiscal registers ~53-60M undercounted; reconstructed mid-Ming population 100-130M)
source: Ho Ping-ti (1959) Studies on the Population of China, 1368-1953, Harvard Univ. Press; Durand (1960) Popul. Stud. 13:209; Brook (1998) The Confusions of Pleasure; Maddison (2001) OECD
note: Ho Ping-ti (1959) showed Ming lijia tax registers (~53-60M) severely underreported households; demographic reconstructions place 1450 CE Ming China at ~100-130M, matching census 1.2e8.

entity_or_polity: Mughal Empire under Aurangzeb & Early Qing Empire under Kangxi
source: Habib (1982) An Atlas of the Mughal Empire; Moosvi (1987) The Economy of the Mughal Empire c. 1595; Ho Ping-ti (1959) Studies on the Population of China; Maddison (2001) OECD
note: Around 1665 CE, Aurangzeb's Mughal Empire (~150M across ~85-90% of the ~165M Indian subcontinent) slightly exceeded early post-transition Qing China (~120-150M); census 1.8e8 sits ~12-20% above the top single empire.

entity_or_polity: Daoguang-era Qing Empire & British Maritime Empire
source: Ho Ping-ti (1959) Studies on the Population of China, 1368-1953, Harvard Univ. Press; Durand (1960) Popul. Stud. 13:209; Taagepera (1997) Int. Stud. Q. 41:475
note: Official Qing baojia population reports reached 414.7 million in 1841 and ~412-422 million in 1844-1848 prior to the Taiping Rebellion, matching census 4.0e8 within 3%.

entity_or_polity: Submarine-telegraph-linked global trade population (single largest polities: Qing China ~380M, British Empire ~345M)
published_estimate_range: 1.52x10^9 global humans in OWID/HYDE (1,520,891,633); largest single empires 3.4x10^8 - 4.0x10^8
source: Klein Goldewijk et al. (2017) HYDE 3.3 / Gapminder / Our World in Data; Maddison (2001) The World Economy, OECD; Taagepera (1997) Int. Stud. Q. 41:475; Standage (1998) The Victorian Internet
note: Ontological switch at 1890 CE: census shifts from 'largest single sovereign state' (~3.8e8 Qing China or ~3.5e8 British Empire in 1890) to 'entire world human population linked by transoceanic telegraph cables and steam shipping' (1.52B in OWID vs 1.50B in census).

entity_or_polity: United Nations / global radio-aviation-linked world population
published_estimate_range: 2.38x10^9 - 2.50x10^9 global humans (OWID 1945 = 2,384,671,779; UN 1950 = 2,493,092,852; largest single empire ~5.5x10^8 British Empire)
source: United Nations (2024) World Population Prospects 2024; Gapminder / HYDE 3.3 via Our World in Data; Maddison (2001) OECD
note: OWID/Gapminder places 1945 world population at 2.385B (reaching 2.50B in 1950); note the 51 founding UN member states in Oct 1945 represented ~1.7B people before decolonization and universal membership.

entity_or_polity: Global human population linked by geostationary satellites, aviation & Cold War blocs
source: United Nations (2024) World Population Prospects 2024; Our World in Data
note: Matches UN World Population Prospects 1965 global population (3.335B) within 1.0%.

entity_or_polity: Global human population linked by fiber-optic cables & the World Wide Web
published_estimate_range: 6.14x10^9 - 6.17x10^9 global humans (UN WPP 2024 / OWID 2000 = 6,171,702,992; active Internet users ~4.0x10^8 in 2000 per ITU)
source: United Nations (2024) World Population Prospects 2024; International Telecommunication Union (ITU) World Telecommunication/ICT Indicators
note: Matches UN 2000 world population (6.17B) within 1.1%; note active Web users were ~6.5% of humanity (~400M) in 2000 while global telecom/trade reached nearly all nation-states.

entity_or_polity: Mobile-connected global human civilization (2010 CE)
published_estimate_range: 6.95x10^9 - 7.02x10^9 global humans (UN WPP 2024 / OWID 2010 = 7,021,732,143; ~2.0x10^9 Internet & ~5.3x10^9 mobile subscriptions per ITU)
source: United Nations (2024) World Population Prospects 2024; ITU (2011) Measuring the Information Society
note: Matches UN 2010 world population (6.95-7.02B across WPP 2019/2024 revisions) within 1.0%.

entity_or_polity: Cloud- and smartphone-connected global human civilization (2012 CE)
published_estimate_range: 7.09x10^9 - 7.20x10^9 global humans (UN WPP 2024 / OWID 2012 = 7,201,202,478; ~2.4x10^9 Internet users per ITU)
source: United Nations (2024) World Population Prospects 2024; ITU (2013) Measuring the Information Society
note: Matches UN 2012 world population (7.10-7.20B across WPP revisions) within 1.4%.

entity_or_polity: Globally networked human civilization during planetary genomic/pandemic coordination (2020 CE)
published_estimate_range: 7.84x10^9 - 7.89x10^9 global humans (UN WPP 2024 / OWID 2020 = 7,887,001,289; ~4.7x10^9 Internet users per ITU)
source: United Nations (2024) World Population Prospects 2024; ITU (2021) Facts and Figures
note: Matches UN 2020 world population (7.89B) within 1.1%.

entity_or_polity: Planetary networked human civilization coupled to ~6.5B silicon devices & AI clusters (2026 CE)
published_estimate_range: 8.09x10^9 (2023) - 8.30x10^9 (2026 UN WPP 2024 medium projection = 8,300,678,396); ~5.5x10^9 active Internet users (ITU 2024)
source: United Nations (2024) World Population Prospects 2024; International Telecommunication Union (2024) Facts and Figures 2024
note: Canonical 8.1e9 headline matches UN WPP 2023-2024 measured baseline (8.09B in 2023, 8.16B in 2024, 8.30B projected in 2026).
